title: The Fall of the House of Usher
focus: a family and a house collapsing together

teacherSummary.text: The narrator answers a letter from his boyhood friend Roderick Usher and visits the gloomy Usher mansion, which has a faint crack running down its front. Roderick suffers from acute senses and dread; his twin Madeline wastes away and is entombed in a vault, apparently dead. Days later, during a storm, she bursts out of her tomb and falls dead on her brother, who dies of terror. The narrator flees as the house splits along the crack and sinks into the tarn.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this story is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “The Fall of the House of Usher,” how does Poe show a family and a house collapsing together? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the setting you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In The Fall of the House of Usher, how does Poe develop the idea of a family and a house collapsing together? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the setting in the story helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how The Fall of the House of Usher develops the idea of a family and a house collapsing together. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of setting and imagery shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of The Fall of the House of Usher (where it begins, turns and ends) and its setting shape the reader's understanding of a family and a house collapsing together. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what The Fall of the House of Usher suggests about a family and a house collapsing together. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's setting and imagery), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Edgar Allan Poe uses setting in The Fall of the House of Usher to complicate the reader's understanding of a family and a house collapsing together. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate The Fall of the House of Usher within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of a family and a house collapsing together responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read The Fall of the House of Usher alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of a family and a house collapsing together follows or bends those conventions, using the setting as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to The Fall of the House of Usher and its treatment of a family and a house collapsing together. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's setting and imagery, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads The Fall of the House of Usher as evidence for a larger claim about a family and a house collapsing together in The Fall of the House of Usher. Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads The Fall of the House of Usher as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of a family and a house collapsing together. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on The Fall of the House of Usher.

satQuestions.passage: The room in which I found myself was very large and lofty. The windows were long, narrow, and pointed, and at so vast a distance from the black oaken floor as to be altogether inaccessible from within. Feeble gleams of encrimsoned light made their way through the trellissed panes, and served to render sufficiently distinct the more prominent objects around; the eye, however, struggled in vain to reach the remoter angles of the chamber, or the recesses of the vaulted and fretted ceiling. Dark draperies hung upon the walls. The general furniture was profuse, comfortless, antique, and tattered. Many books and musical instruments lay scattered about, but failed to give any vitality to the scene. I felt that I breathed an atmosphere of sorrow. An air of stern, deep, and irredeemable gloom hung over and pervaded all.

A family and a house collapsing together
Superstition used against a credulous man
A reversal that punishes a change of heart

literaryElements.label: Setting

Watch for the fissure: the hairline crack that splits the house at the end: a hidden flaw in the family and in Roderick's mind.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Sensitive content: Premature burial; gothic dread. Preview the story, tell students in advance, and allow a pass on reading aloud. Keep discussion on how the writer uses these elements, not on graphic detail.
